en: *Satyadvayāvatāra-nāma* (Entry into the Two Truths).
Homage to the Great Compassionate One!
The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths:
the conventional truth of the world and the truth of the ultimate meaning.
Conventional reality is considered to be twofold: the false and suchness.
The former is of two kinds: the moon in water and the conceptualization of flawed tenets.
That which is delightful only when not analyzed, which possesses the nature of arising and perishing,
and which is capable of causal efficiency, is considered conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) in relation to suchness (*tathatā*).
For the ultimate reality is indeed one alone, yet it is considered twofold by others;
since no such nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is established, how could there be two, three, or more?
Characterized by teachings such as non-arising and non-ceasing,
because its nature is non-different from the ultimate truth, there are neither phenomena nor the nature of phenomena.
In emptiness, not even the slightest distinction exists;
because it is free from conceptual construction, the vision of emptiness is said to be awakening.
It is said in the profoundly deep Sūtra: "The seeing of that is non-seeing;
therein neither a seer nor a seen exists—[that which is] auspicious, without beginning or end."
Non-conceptual, without support, devoid of existence and non-existence,
without basis or foundation, incomparable, and free from coming and going.
Ineffable, without appearance, changeless, and unconditioned,
this is accessible to yogis and free from the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable.
"Direct perception and inference—these two are accepted by the Buddhists;
emptiness is to be understood through both"—this is the speech of those with limited vision and delusion. (Sda 10)
The knowledge of the nature of phenomena (dharmatājñāna) would follow as a consequence for non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, and even for the Vijñānavādins;
what then need be said regarding its lack of contradiction in the Madhyamaka?

In that case, all philosophical tenets would be equal in being objects of valid cognition; for even the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) as an object of cognition is contradicted by every form of reasoning. (Sda 12)

How could it not be direct perception for the most part? And why would inference be useless? The learned have composed these treatises for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of the non-Buddhist outsiders. (Sda 13)
It is not apprehended by either conceptual or non-conceptual cognitions;
this has been clearly stated even in the scriptures by the learned master Ācārya Bhavya.
By whom was that emptiness, which was prophesied by the Tathāgatas, understood?
It was indeed Nāgāntevāsicandra, the seer of the truth of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

Thereafter, through the successive lineages of oral transmission, the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma were taught as being accessible through the truth of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Sda_16.

Everything is included within the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); liberation arises from the realization of emptiness, and for that purpose, all other meditations are practiced by relying upon conventional truth.
When there is the practice of emptiness, one who does not understand the meaning of solitude is deceived regarding the causes of conventional reality, such as merit, and regarding the next world.
That man who relies on very little learning and performs no meritorious deeds is lost;
he is a base person, and his wrong views bring about destruction.
Candrācārya spoke thus to those of dull intellect:
"Conventional truth is the means, and ultimate truth is the goal. (Sda 20)
He who does not know the distinction between these two will go to ruin due to his perverted understanding.
Without resorting to conventional truth, the ultimate truth cannot be taught.
Without the ladder of correct conventional reality, it is not possible for the wise to ascend to the pinnacle of the palace of ultimate truth.
Just as this appearance of conventional reality is not found at all when analyzed through reasoning,
so too the ultimate truth is non-finding— the dharmatā that has been established from the very beginning.
Because it is produced from causes and conditions, the conventional is considered to be like a reflection;
if you think it is improper to purify that which is fashioned like the moon in water and so forth, [then consider this].
Therefore, because it is produced by various conditions, every appearance is established;
yet, due to the cessation of those conditions, even from the perspective of conventional reality, its occurrence is impossible.
Thus, when the purification of conduct has arisen from the non-delusion regarding views,
one will avoid the wrong path and attain the Akaniṣṭha abode.
Life is short and sciences are many; we do not know what the measure of our lifespan may be.
One should obtain only that which is desired, just as swans extract milk from the midst of water.
Even for one with limited vision, due to the power of delusion, it is not possible to determine the two truths even by relying here upon the words of the masters;
for the duality that has been posited does not accord with the truth of the scriptures.
If, out of deference to the king, gold has been produced here on Suvarṇadvīpa, let a person who is faithful today accept it after thorough examination, and not merely out of faith or out of respect.
For the monk Devamati was sent by the King of Suvarṇa as a fruit of his devotion to the Guru;
therefore, through his authority, the entry into the two truths should be examined here by the wise using reasoning. (Sda 30)
The *Satyadvayāvatāra* (Introduction to the Two Truths), composed by the master Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, is completed.
It was translated and finalized after being edited by that same scholar, the translator Vīryasiṃha.
